notes:
Docket told a newsroom that its co-publishing agreement was probably an accident.

When a page's canonical tag points at a different domain, Docket reports it at the highest severity it has. That is usually right: a canonical leaving your site hands the ranking to somebody else, and the cause is nearly always a copied template or a staging URL nobody removed. The finding said so, and told you to take the canonical back.

Nearly always is not always.

Investigative newsrooms co-publish. A story is reported jointly, it runs on both outlets, and the partner takes the canonical by agreement. We found five of them on a single nonprofit newsroom — stories canonicalising to a state newspaper and to a metro daily — and every one of those pages says what it is, in the byline, beside the reporters' names: "Co-published with" the same outlet the canonical points at.

Docket called that a probable accident and advised undoing it. A newsroom that followed the advice would have broken an agreement with another newsroom and put two outlets into competition for one story.

So Docket now reads what the page says. When a page's own text declares the arrangement — co-published with, originally published by, in partnership with — and names the very domain its canonical points at, that is not a stray tag, and Docket no longer calls it one.

**It still tells you what it costs.** The canonical really does hand the ranking for that story to your partner, and searches for your own reporting can land on their copy. That is worth knowing whether or not you meant it. The advice is now the true one: nothing here is broken; if the arrangement is what you intend, leave it; and if you would rather keep the ranking, Google does not recommend the canonical element for syndication at all — agreeing which outlet takes the canonical story by story, or asking the partner to noindex their copy, are the arrangements that actually work.

**Both halves are required, so a genuine leak is still reported at full severity.** A copied template has no such sentence, and a leaked staging URL has neither the sentence nor a matching name — nobody writes "co-published with" about a domain they exposed by mistake. A page that mentions one outlet while canonicalising to an unrelated host is still reported as the accident it is.

One detail worth recording, because it is the kind of thing that quietly produces a wrong answer. The newsroom also embeds a ready-made republishing block — a canonical tag and a syndication tag for other outlets to copy — inside a text box on the page. Those are characters in a form field, not instructions to a search engine. Docket reads the parsed page, so it never mistook them for the page's own declaration; a plain text search of the same HTML finds them and would.
